metadata.title: Product Streams
metadata.description: Outcome-based product streams for the Tour Operator ERP Platform domain: the travel trade lifecycle Product -> Sell -> Book -> Operate -> Serve -> Settle -> Steer as run by group and coach tour operators, tailor-made specialists and DMCs on the combined 1TIS + TravelSpirit platform, plus the marketing, reseller distribution and insight journeys that hang off it.
metadata.flowModelNote: Each stream carries only stream-specific flows, names the supporting bricks used in each step and the persona acting in it, and lists the external systems (payment provider, accounting, GDS/BSP, guarantee fund, marketing, review and partner-app platforms) the flow depends on.

rootGroups.name: Product and Sales Journeys
rootGroups.description: From supplier contracts to sellable products and from a travel wish or website visit to a confirmed booking: the journeys that bring revenue into the travel organisation through the desk, the website and the Visual Tour Builder.

streams.name: Build and Price Travel Products
streams.description: Take a travel organisation from negotiated supplier contracts to sellable packages, fixed-date departures, series and individual components with prices, yield rules and group calculations, so that every channel — desk, website, reseller portal and Visual Tour Builder — sells from one product master instead of a brochure spreadsheet.
outcomes: One product master feeds every sales channel, so prices and availability never diverge between brochure, website and desk
Departure margins are known before the first booking, because group calculations tie purchase cost, minimum participants and yield tiers together
Seasonal product setup takes days instead of weeks, with contracts, content and pricing reused across seasons

flows.title: Contract, Compose and Price a Group Departure Series
flows.description: From a hotel and coach contract to a published series of fixed-date departures with tiered yield pricing and minimum-participant rules.
flows.trigger: The season's purchasing round closes and contracted rates arrive from hotels, coach companies and DMCs.
flows.successSignal: The series is live on the website with correct prices, capacity and cancellation deadlines per departure.

steps.title: Register supplier contracts and purchase rates
keyFacts: A coach round trip typically combines one coach contract, six to ten hotel contracts, ferry or toll components and a local DMC agreement per departure.
Contracts carry allotments, release dates, child and single-room supplements and currency, all of which drive the group calculation later.
painPoints: Contract terms living in email attachments mean release dates are missed and rooms are paid for that were never sold.
Re-keying the same hotel rates into a purchase sheet and a sales sheet is the top source of margin errors.

dependencies.name: Purchasing and Supplier Contracts
dependencies.description: Stores supplier contracts, allotments and release dates.
dependencies.how: Captures each contract once as the purchasing basis for every product that uses it.

dependencies.name: Supplier Management and Communication
dependencies.description: Supplier master data and communication history.
dependencies.how: Links the contract to the supplier record and its contacts.

steps.title: Compose components and inventory
keyFacts: A component is a reusable accommodation, transport or activity block with its own availability, so a hotel night can be used in a group series and in a tailor-made itinerary alike.
Allotment and on-request components behave differently at booking time: allotment sells immediately, on-request needs a supplier confirmation.
painPoints: Duplicated components per product make a single hotel rate change a multi-hour edit.
Unclear allotment versus on-request status leads agents to confirm rooms that do not exist.

dependencies.name: Components, Inventory and Availability
dependencies.description: Reusable components with inventory and availability.
dependencies.how: Turns contract lines into bookable components with allotment rules.

dependencies.name: Bed-Bank and Supplier Content Feeds
dependencies.description: Live accommodation and activity content that feeds components, availability and pricing.
dependencies.interface: Availability, rate and content APIs
dependencies.how: Pulls live bed-bank content and rates for components not covered by a direct contract.

steps.title: Build the package and day-by-day itinerary
keyFacts: A package fixes the sequence of components per day and the inclusions and exclusions shown to the traveler.
Package templates are cloned per season so that only dates, prices and changed hotels need editing.
painPoints: Itineraries copied by hand into the website CMS drift from what operations actually runs.
Inclusion texts written per product instead of per component are inconsistent across the catalogue.

dependencies.name: Travel Products and Packages
dependencies.how: Assembles components into a sellable package with itinerary and inclusions.

dependencies.name: Travel Content and Media Management
dependencies.description: Photos, texts and media per product and destination.
dependencies.how: Attaches destination texts and MediaSpirit-style photo sets to the package.

steps.title: Generate the departure series with capacity
keyFacts: A series generates fixed-date departures from a rhythm (for example every Saturday from April to October) with capacity per departure derived from coach size and hotel allotments.

Each departure carries a minimum number of participants; under the Package Travel Directive the operator must cancel at least 20 days before departure for trips longer than six days if that minimum is not met.
painPoints: Creating departures one by one invites date and capacity typos that surface only when a bus is overbooked.
Minimum-participant deadlines tracked in a wall calendar are missed, exposing the operator to full refunds.

dependencies.name: Departures and Capacity Management
dependencies.description: Departures with capacity, minimums and deadlines.
dependencies.how: Generates the departure series and stores capacity and go/no-go deadlines.

steps.title: Run the group calculation and set tiered yield prices
keyFacts: The group calculation divides fixed costs (coach, guide, ferry) over the expected participant count and adds variable costs per person to reach a break-even and target-margin price.
Yield tiers raise or lower the price by departure and by booking window, for example an early-bird price until a fixed date and a higher price when the bus is more than 80% full.
painPoints: Calculations kept in personal spreadsheets cannot be reproduced when finance asks why a departure lost money.
Manual price updates per departure lag behind demand, so full buses are sold at early-bird prices.

dependencies.name: Pricing, Yield and Group Calculations
dependencies.description: Pricing, yield rules and group calculations.
dependencies.how: Computes break-even, target-margin and tiered prices per departure.

steps.title: Review margin and approve the product for sale
keyFacts: The owner sees expected margin per departure at the minimum, break-even and full-bus scenario before a single seat is sold.
Approval locks the price list and cancellation deadlines that finance and the website will use.
painPoints: Without a scenario view, owners approve products that only break even at a full bus.
Late price corrections after publication create different prices for the same departure across channels.

dependencies.name: Pricing, Yield and Group Calculations
dependencies.how: Presents minimum, break-even and full-capacity margin for approval.

dependencies.name: Travel Products and Packages
dependencies.how: Sets the product to sellable once approved.

steps.title: Publish to website, desk and reseller channels
keyFacts: Publication pushes the same product, prices and real-time availability to the customer website, the booking desk and the reseller portal.
Content, price and availability changes after publication propagate automatically instead of via a CMS edit.
painPoints: A separately maintained website catalogue is the main reason customers see a price that the desk cannot honour.
Unpublished changes to inclusions cause complaints when the trip differs from what was sold.

dependencies.name: Customer Website, CMS and Online Booking
dependencies.how: Renders the approved product with live prices and availability.

dependencies.name: Travel Products and Packages
dependencies.description: Product master as the single source for all channels.
dependencies.how: Distributes one product definition to every channel.

flows.title: Maintain Components and Content for Tailor-Made Selling
flows.description: Keep the component library, sample itineraries and media current so specialists can compose proposals from stored, correctly priced building blocks.
flows.trigger: A destination manager receives new season rates from lodges, transfers and excursions in a destination.
flows.successSignal: Every component in the destination has valid rates, content and photos for the coming season and appears in the Visual Tour Builder.

steps.title: Update destination component rates and validity
keyFacts: Tailor-made specialists maintain hundreds of lodges, transfers and excursions per destination, each with seasonal rate bands and validity dates.
Rates are held in supplier currency and converted at booking with a configurable margin on the exchange rate.
painPoints: Rate sheets in PDF are re-typed per season, which is where wrong nights and wrong seasons creep in.
Missing validity dates make expired rates appear in proposals for next year.

dependencies.name: Components, Inventory and Availability
dependencies.how: Stores rate bands per season and currency.

dependencies.name: Purchasing and Supplier Contracts
dependencies.description: Supplier contract terms behind the rates.
dependencies.how: Keeps the contractual basis for each rate band.

steps.title: Curate destination content and photos
keyFacts: Each component carries description texts in the tenant's languages and a curated photo set that the Visual Tour Builder places into proposals automatically.
Photo rights and supplier-provided imagery are tracked per asset so that proposals never use unlicensed images.
painPoints: Specialists searching shared drives for photos spend more time on layout than on the itinerary.
Outdated lodge photos are the leading cause of 'this is not what we booked' complaints.

dependencies.name: Travel Content and Media Management
dependencies.description: Content and media library per component.
dependencies.how: Provides the texts and photos that proposals reuse.

steps.title: Build sample itineraries as starting points
keyFacts: A sample itinerary is a stored sequence of components — for example a 14-day Tanzania safari — used as the first draft for most requests.
Sample itineraries are also published to the website as inspiration and are directly requestable by the traveler.
painPoints: Every proposal started from a blank page is slower and less consistent than one started from a template.
Samples that are not re-priced each season mislead customers on the website.

dependencies.name: Travel Products and Packages
dependencies.description: Products that wrap sample itineraries for publication.
dependencies.how: Publishes samples as requestable products.

steps.title: Set margin and pricing rules per component type
keyFacts: Margin targets differ per component type — accommodation, international flights and local transfers rarely carry the same markup.
Rules can also apply per customer segment or reseller so that agent bookings automatically carry the agreed commission.
painPoints: Margins applied by hand in each proposal vary per specialist and are hard to audit.
A single wrong markup rule silently underprices a whole destination.

dependencies.name: Pricing, Yield and Group Calculations
dependencies.how: Applies configurable margins per component type and channel.

steps.title: Verify supplier payment and cancellation terms
keyFacts: Supplier cancellation terms determine the operator's own cancellation ladder toward the traveler under the Package Travel Directive.
Prepayment requirements per supplier drive the cash-flow planning for the season.
painPoints: Unknown supplier deadlines turn every customer cancellation into a negotiation.
Prepayment obligations not visible to finance cause surprise outflows.

dependencies.name: Purchasing and Supplier Contracts
dependencies.how: Records cancellation ladders and prepayment obligations.

dependencies.name: Supplier Management and Communication
dependencies.how: Keeps the accountable supplier contact for each term.

steps.title: Release the destination library to the builder and website
keyFacts: Released components become draggable blocks in the Visual Tour Builder and searchable on the SPoE website.
Release checks flag components without price, photo or validity before they reach a proposal.
painPoints: Incomplete components discovered during a customer call embarrass the specialist.
Unreleased updates leave the website showing last year's itineraries.

dependencies.name: Customer Website, CMS and Online Booking
dependencies.how: Publishes released content on the website.

streams.name: Quote and Sell Tailor-Made Trips
streams.description: Take a tailor-made specialist from an inbound travel wish to an accepted visual proposal and an opened trip file: capture the lead in the CRM, compose a day-by-day itinerary by dragging stored components into the Visual Tour Builder, price it at target margin, publish the proposal online for the client to review and approve, iterate on changes, and convert the accepted proposal into a booking file without re-entering a single line.
outcomes: Proposal turnaround measured in hours rather than days, because itineraries are composed from priced components and sample trips
Higher proposal acceptance, because clients review a visual, photo-rich itinerary online and approve it with one click
Every accepted proposal becomes a trip file at the calculated margin, with no re-keying between quote and booking

flows.title: From Travel Wish to Approved Visual Proposal
flows.description: The core Visual Tour Builder flow: qualify the lead, compose and price the itinerary, publish it online and convert the approval into a trip file.
flows.trigger: A traveler submits a request form on the website or calls with a wish such as 'three weeks Namibia self-drive in October for a family of four'.
flows.successSignal: The client approves the proposal online, pays the deposit and a trip file exists with all components and the target margin.

steps.title: Capture and qualify the travel wish
keyFacts: Website request forms, inbound email and phone calls land as leads on the contact record, with travel dates, party, budget and interests captured in structured fields.
Inbound email and calls are matched to the contact automatically, so the specialist sees earlier trips and open proposals before answering.
painPoints: Leads spread over personal mailboxes are followed up late or twice.
Unstructured wishes force a second call before any drafting can start.

dependencies.name: CRM and Contact Management
dependencies.how: Creates the lead against the contact with structured wish data.

dependencies.name: Email and Telephony Integration
dependencies.description: Email and telephony linked to the contact.
dependencies.how: Attaches the inbound email or call to the lead.

dependencies.name: WeCloudIT Email and Telephony
dependencies.description: Links inbound email and calls to the contact and booking file that the agent is working on.
dependencies.interface: Mailbox sync and click-to-dial / caller identification
dependencies.how: Identifies the caller and opens the matching contact during the call.

steps.title: Draft a first outline with the AI assistant
keyFacts: The AI office assistant reads the wish and proposes a route outline and candidate sample itineraries from the tenant's own library, not from the open internet.
The specialist keeps full control: the assistant suggests, the human composes and prices.
painPoints: Blank-page drafting is the slowest part of the specialist's day.
Generic AI text that ignores the operator's own stock of lodges creates proposals that cannot be delivered.

dependencies.name: AI Office Assistants
dependencies.how: Suggests routes and sample itineraries matching the wish.

dependencies.name: Visual Tour Builder, Quotes and Itineraries
dependencies.how: Loads the chosen sample itinerary as the first draft.

steps.title: Compose the day-by-day itinerary by drag and drop
keyFacts: Stored components — lodges, transfers, excursions, flights — are dragged onto a day-by-day canvas; texts and photos come along automatically.
Availability and rate validity are checked per component as it is placed, so the draft is buildable from the start.
painPoints: Word documents assembled from copied text and photos take hours and look different per specialist.
Components dragged in without an availability check produce proposals that fall apart on confirmation.

dependencies.name: Visual Tour Builder, Quotes and Itineraries
dependencies.how: Places components on the day canvas with text and media.

dependencies.name: Components, Inventory and Availability
dependencies.how: Validates each placed component against inventory and validity.

steps.title: Price the proposal at target margin
keyFacts: The calculation sums supplier costs in their currencies, applies margin rules per component type and shows the resulting margin against the target before the price is shown to the client.
Optional items and alternative lodges can be priced as choices the client toggles online.
painPoints: Margins computed by hand in a side spreadsheet differ from the eventual invoice.
Specialists under sales pressure quietly give margin away without visibility for the owner.

dependencies.name: Pricing, Yield and Group Calculations
dependencies.how: Calculates cost, margin and sales price per line and in total.

dependencies.name: Visual Tour Builder, Quotes and Itineraries
dependencies.how: Shows the specialist the margin and the client the price.

steps.title: Publish the proposal for online review
keyFacts: The proposal is published as a personal web page with maps, photos, day texts and price, and a link is emailed to the client.
Views and time-on-page are tracked so the specialist knows when to follow up.
painPoints: PDF proposals cannot be updated after sending and are read on a phone with difficulty.
Specialists follow up blind, without knowing whether the client opened the proposal.

dependencies.name: Visual Tour Builder, Quotes and Itineraries
dependencies.how: Renders the itinerary as a personal web page and tracks views.

dependencies.name: Traveler Portal and My-Trip App
dependencies.description: Traveler portal where proposals are reviewed.
dependencies.how: Presents the proposal in the client's personal environment.

steps.title: Iterate on client feedback
keyFacts: Clients comment per day or component in the portal; the specialist swaps a lodge or adds a night and republishes as a new version.
Version history keeps every proposal variant with its price so a client can return to an earlier option.
painPoints: Changes exchanged by email get lost, and the final trip differs from what the client remembers.
Re-pricing a change by hand takes longer than the change itself.

dependencies.name: Visual Tour Builder, Quotes and Itineraries
dependencies.how: Applies changes and republishes a versioned proposal.

dependencies.name: Pricing, Yield and Group Calculations
dependencies.how: Recomputes price and margin for every version.

steps.title: Client approves online and pays the deposit
keyFacts: The client approves the proposal with one click, accepts the travel conditions and pays the deposit via a payment link in the same session.
Acceptance timestamps and accepted conditions are stored as the contract record required under the Package Travel Directive.
painPoints: Approval by email reply and a separate bank transfer delays the confirmation by days.
Missing proof of accepted conditions weakens the operator's position in disputes.

dependencies.name: Traveler Portal and My-Trip App
dependencies.description: Approval and payment in the traveler portal.
dependencies.how: Records the approval and triggers the deposit payment.

steps.title: Convert the accepted proposal into a trip file
keyFacts: Conversion creates the booking file with every component as a booking line, the calculated margin and the supplier requests still to be sent.
The proposal remains linked to the file so later changes are traceable to what was sold.
painPoints: Re-keying accepted proposals into the booking system is where names, dates and prices get corrupted.
Unlinked proposals make it impossible to compare sold margin with realised margin.

streams.name: Book Online and at the Desk
streams.description: Take an inquiry from the website, phone or email to a confirmed booking with deposit paid — whether the traveler completes the booking on the real-time customer website or the reservations agent books in the back office. Both paths use the same product master, capacity, seat map and price rules, so a web booking and a desk booking are indistinguishable in the file.
outcomes: Higher online booking share, because the website sells real-time availability and prices from the back office instead of a request form
Bookings confirmed in one contact at the desk, with capacity, seats, price and deposit handled in the same screen
Zero re-keying between website, desk and booking file, so options, changes and payments carry the same data

flows.title: Traveler Books a Group Departure on the Real-Time Website
flows.description: A traveler finds a coach or group tour, picks a departure, chooses a bus seat and room type, pays the deposit and receives the confirmation — with the booking file created in the back office at the same moment.
flows.trigger: A traveler lands on the operator's website looking for a spring coach tour to Tuscany.
flows.successSignal: The booking file is confirmed, the deposit is received via a payment link and the traveler has the confirmation in the my-trip portal.

steps.title: Search the catalogue and select a departure
keyFacts: The website shows the departure calendar with live availability and the price tier valid at that moment for each date.
Departures below minimum participants show as bookable but carry the guaranteed/not-yet-guaranteed status transparently.
painPoints: Websites that show brochure prices and 'request availability' convert far worse than real-time booking.
Hidden 'not guaranteed' status leads to angry customers when a departure is cancelled.

dependencies.name: Customer Website, CMS and Online Booking
dependencies.how: Renders products and departures with live prices.

dependencies.name: Departures and Capacity Management
dependencies.how: Provides seats left and guarantee status per date.

steps.title: Choose a bus seat and room type
keyFacts: The seat map of the assigned coach is shown at booking; travelers pick their seat and the seat is reserved immediately — a 1TIS hallmark for coach operators.
Room types (double, single with supplement, triple) reduce hotel allotment per night as they are chosen.
painPoints: Seat allocation done later by phone generates a wave of calls in the week before departure.
Selling room types without allotment checks overbooks single rooms that hotels cannot supply.

dependencies.name: Seat and Room Allocation
dependencies.how: Reserves the chosen seat and room at booking.

dependencies.name: Components, Inventory and Availability
dependencies.how: Decrements the room allotment for the selected type.

steps.title: Enter traveler details, wishes and extras
keyFacts: Passenger names as in the passport, dietary wishes and mobility needs are captured at booking so they flow to room lists and guides without a later call.
Extras such as insurance, excursions or an eSIM are offered as priced options.
painPoints: Dietary wishes collected later by email arrive too late for the hotel.
Insurance and excursions sold separately by phone are margin left on the table.

dependencies.name: Customer Website, CMS and Online Booking
dependencies.description: Booking form with passengers and extras.
dependencies.how: Captures passenger data, wishes and options.

steps.title: Accept conditions and pay the deposit
keyFacts: The traveler accepts the package travel conditions and the SGR guarantee is shown before payment, as required for package sales in the Netherlands.
Deposit is paid in the same session via iDEAL or card through a hosted payment link.
painPoints: Bookings that wait for a bank transfer are abandoned or double-booked in the meantime.
Missing evidence of accepted conditions costs the operator disputes.

dependencies.name: Invoicing, Payment Links and Collection
dependencies.how: Creates the deposit request and records the payment.

dependencies.name: Mollie Payment Platform
dependencies.description: Hosted payment links and status webhooks for deposits, balances and refunds.
dependencies.interface: Payment links, iDEAL, cards and webhooks
dependencies.how: Handles the online deposit payment and confirms it via webhook.

steps.title: Create the booking file and confirm
keyFacts: The booking file is created in the back office in real time with status confirmed, the seat, room, passengers, price tier and payment already attached.
A contact record is created or matched, so the traveler's history starts here.
painPoints: Website bookings that arrive as email to be re-keyed are the number-one source of desk errors.
Duplicate contacts created per booking make marketing and history useless.

dependencies.name: Booking Files and Dossiers
dependencies.how: Stores the confirmed booking as the system of record.

dependencies.name: CRM and Contact Management
dependencies.how: Links the booking to a single contact record.

steps.title: Send confirmation and my-trip access
keyFacts: The confirmation email contains the invoice, the balance due date and a link to the traveler portal where documents will appear.
Workflow rules schedule the balance reminder and passenger-data completion tasks automatically.
painPoints: Confirmations typed by hand are inconsistent and miss legal information.
Follow-up tasks left to memory are the reason balances go unpaid.

dependencies.name: Workflow, Tasks and Alerts
dependencies.how: Schedules reminders and data-completion tasks.

dependencies.name: Email and Telephony Integration
dependencies.how: Sends and logs the confirmation.

steps.title: Monitor the capacity and yield effect
keyFacts: Each booking updates the departure's load factor and may trigger the next price tier or the minimum-participant threshold.
Operations sees departures approaching full, so a second coach or hotel allotment increase can be arranged in time.
painPoints: Capacity checked once a week misses the moment to add a coach.
Price tiers switched by hand lag behind demand.

dependencies.name: Departures and Capacity Management
dependencies.description: Load factor and thresholds per departure.
dependencies.how: Updates capacity and flags thresholds crossed.

dependencies.name: Pricing, Yield and Group Calculations
dependencies.how: Applies the next price tier when the rule fires.

flows.title: Agent Books at the Desk from a Phone Inquiry
flows.description: A reservations agent turns a phone or email inquiry into an option or confirmed booking in one contact, including flights imported from the GDS and a payment link sent during the call.
flows.trigger: A customer calls about a group trip seen in the brochure and wants to book for two with a specific seat and a flight from Amsterdam.
flows.successSignal: The booking is confirmed in the same call, the payment link is paid and the customer receives the confirmation before hanging up.

steps.title: Identify the caller and open the contact
keyFacts: Caller identification opens the contact record and any open options before the agent says hello.
Inbound emails are attached to the contact and can be turned into a booking with one action.
painPoints: Agents asking 'have you booked with us before' start every call on the back foot.
Emails in personal inboxes are handled twice or not at all.

dependencies.name: CRM and Contact Management
dependencies.how: Shows the caller's history and open items.

dependencies.name: Email and Telephony Integration
dependencies.how: Pops the contact on the call.

dependencies.name: WeCloudIT Email and Telephony
dependencies.description: Links inbound email and calls to the contact and booking file that the agent is working on.
dependencies.interface: Mailbox sync and click-to-dial / caller identification
dependencies.how: Delivers caller identification and the click-to-dial link to the contact.

steps.title: Check availability, seat and price in one screen
keyFacts: The agent sees the same availability, seat map and price tier the website shows, plus agent-only options such as manual discounts within limits.
Alternative departures are suggested when the requested one is full.
painPoints: Switching between a brochure, a capacity sheet and a seat drawing takes minutes per call.
Agents quoting a price different from the website destroy trust.

dependencies.name: Departures and Capacity Management
dependencies.how: Shows seats left and status per departure.

dependencies.name: Seat and Room Allocation
dependencies.how: Lets the agent reserve the requested seat.

steps.title: Place an option or a confirmed booking
keyFacts: Options hold capacity and seat for a configurable period and expire automatically, releasing the seat.
A confirmed booking creates the file with passengers, wishes and extras captured during the call.
painPoints: Options never released block seats that could have been sold.
Bookings written on paper and entered later lose the seat to a web booking in between.

dependencies.name: Booking Files and Dossiers
dependencies.how: Creates the file with option expiry or confirmed status.

dependencies.name: Workflow, Tasks and Alerts
dependencies.how: Expires options and releases capacity automatically.

steps.title: Import flights from the GDS or Airtrade
keyFacts: Flight segments booked in the GDS or through the Airtrade consolidator are imported by PNR into the booking file with fare, taxes and ticketing deadline.
The ticketing deadline becomes a task so the ticket is issued before the fare expires.
painPoints: Flight details typed from a GDS screen produce wrong times on travel documents.
Missed ticketing deadlines cost the fare and the customer's trust.

dependencies.name: Flight Import and Ticket Settlement

steps.title: Send the payment link during the call
keyFacts: A deposit payment link is sent by email or SMS while the customer is on the line, and the payment status appears in the file within seconds.
Paid deposit flips the booking from option to confirmed without agent action.
painPoints: Waiting for a transfer means calling back days later to confirm.
Manual payment matching delays confirmation even when the customer paid immediately.

steps.title: Confirm and log the contact
keyFacts: Confirmation, invoice and portal invitation go out automatically; the call and its outcome are logged on the contact.
Any follow-up (passport data, seat change request) becomes a task with an owner and due date.
painPoints: Unlogged calls mean the next agent cannot answer 'what did we agree'.
Follow-ups in sticky notes are lost.

rootGroups.name: Operations and Supply Journeys
rootGroups.description: The journeys that turn confirmed bookings into delivered trips: group departure operations with seats, rooms, guides and lists, and the request-confirm-change loop with suppliers and DMCs.

streams.name: Operate Group Departures
streams.description: Take a group tour operator from a set of confirmed bookings to an executed departure: decide go/no-go against minimum participants and the Package Travel Directive deadlines, allocate bus seats and hotel rooms, send room lists with dietary wishes to hotels and seating lists to the coach company, assign the guide or group leader and give them the participant list in their portal, and keep all lists correct as late bookings and changes arrive.
outcomes: Fewer operational hours per departure, because seat, room, guide and passenger lists are generated from the booking files instead of rebuilt by hand
Higher departure load factor and fewer cancelled departures, thanks to timely go/no-go decisions and yield actions
Accurate room lists and dietary information at every hotel, with changes propagated the moment a booking changes

flows.title: From Capacity Decision to Departure Day
flows.description: The end-to-end operations flow for a fixed-date group departure, from the go/no-go decision through lists and portals to the day the coach leaves.
flows.trigger: The minimum-participant deadline for a departure approaches and the departure dashboard flags it for decision.
flows.successSignal: The coach leaves with a seating list, every hotel has a correct room list, and the guide has the participant list and documents in the portal.

steps.title: Decide go/no-go against minimum participants
keyFacts: The departure dashboard shows bookings versus the minimum, the legal cancellation deadline (20 days before departure for trips over six days, 7 days for two-to-six-day trips, 48 hours for shorter trips) and the margin at the current load.
Operators often guarantee a departure below minimum when margin allows, or merge two departures to fill one coach.
painPoints: Deadlines tracked outside the system lead to late cancellations and full refund obligations under the Package Travel Directive.
Cancelling a departure that would have filled with the last two weeks of bookings loses revenue and reputation.

dependencies.name: Departures and Capacity Management
dependencies.how: Presents the decision data and records the go/no-go.

dependencies.name: Workflow, Tasks and Alerts
dependencies.how: Raises the decision task before the legal deadline.

steps.title: Rebook or merge participants if a departure is cancelled
keyFacts: Participants of a cancelled departure are offered an alternative date or a full refund; rebooking moves the file including seat and room wishes.
Merging two departures re-runs seat and room allocation for the combined group.
painPoints: Rebooking by phone without moving the file duplicates bookings.
Refunds processed late breach the 14-day refund rule of the Package Travel Directive.

steps.title: Allocate bus seats and hotel rooms
keyFacts: Seats reserved at booking are checked against the final coach; travelers who did not choose are placed by rule (couples together, mobility needs in front).
Room allocation groups passengers per booking into the room types sold and flags mismatches against the hotel allotment.
painPoints: Seat drawings on paper are redone for every late change.
Room lists that do not match the sold room types cause check-in chaos.

Hotels with portal access download the current list themselves and confirm it; others receive it by email from the supplier record.
painPoints: Room lists assembled in Excel per hotel are the most error-prone document in group travel.
Dietary wishes lost between booking and hotel are the most common complaint on tour.

Pickup points and times per passenger are derived from the booking, so the driver list is right by construction.
painPoints: Drivers working from an outdated list leave passengers at the wrong pickup.
Coach companies re-typing passenger lists into their own system introduce errors.

Sharing full passenger data by email violates privacy expectations.

Actual participant counts unknown to finance delay supplier settlement.

streams.name: Request and Confirm Supplier Services
streams.description: Take booking lines — an on-request lodge, a DMC ground package, a private transfer, a group's hotel block — to confirmed supplier services with every request, confirmation, rejection and change logged against the file. Suppliers and DMCs work in a portal or by structured email; changes on the operator side propagate one to one to the supplier, and supplier responses update the file without re-keying.
outcomes: Faster supplier confirmation, because requests are generated from the file and answered in a portal rather than composed and parsed by hand
Fewer change errors between operator and DMC, because every change is a versioned delta on the same request
Complete communication history per booking line, so anyone can see what was requested, confirmed and changed

flows.title: Request, Confirm and Sync Services with a DMC
flows.description: A tour operator sends the ground services of a group departure to its destination management company, the DMC confirms in the portal, and later changes flow both ways.
flows.trigger: A group departure is guaranteed and the operator releases the ground-services request to the DMC.
flows.successSignal: All ground services are confirmed by the DMC, the file shows confirmed status per line, and later changes are acknowledged in the portal.

steps.title: Generate service requests from the booking lines
keyFacts: Every on-request or DMC line on the file becomes a structured service request: service, dates, pax, room types, special wishes and the contracted rate.
Requests are bundled per supplier and per departure so the DMC receives one request set, not twenty emails.
painPoints: Requests written by hand omit the detail the supplier needs and trigger a round of questions.
Requests sent per booking overwhelm DMCs with fragments they must consolidate.

dependencies.name: Supplier Management and Communication
dependencies.how: Creates structured requests per supplier.

dependencies.name: Purchasing and Supplier Contracts
dependencies.how: Attaches the agreed rate to each request.

steps.title: Deliver the request via portal, email or API
keyFacts: Portal suppliers get a notification and see the request in their work list; email suppliers receive a structured message; API-connected suppliers receive it machine to machine.
Delivery and read status are tracked so the operator knows what is pending.
painPoints: Unread requests discovered a week later derail the timeline.
Suppliers without a portal still need a clear, complete request.

dependencies.name: Supplier and DMC Portal
dependencies.how: Shows the request to the DMC and tracks its status.

dependencies.name: Integration Hub and Partner APIs
dependencies.how: Delivers requests to API-connected suppliers.

steps.title: The DMC reviews and confirms or rejects each service
keyFacts: The DMC confirms each line, adds a supplier reference and can propose an alternative (different lodge, changed time) instead of rejecting.
Confirmation captures the DMC's own cancellation terms per service.
painPoints: Confirmations by free-text email have to be interpreted and typed into the file.
Alternatives offered by phone are lost and re-requested.

dependencies.name: Supplier and DMC Portal
dependencies.how: Records confirm, reject or alternative per line with references.

steps.title: Update the file and notify the operator
keyFacts: Confirmed lines flip to confirmed on the file with the supplier reference; rejections and alternatives create a task for the operator.
Travel documents can only be issued when all lines are confirmed, which the workflow enforces.
painPoints: Files that show 'requested' forever hide the risk of unconfirmed services.
Documents issued with unconfirmed services lead to travelers standing at closed doors.

dependencies.name: Booking Files and Dossiers
dependencies.how: Updates line status from supplier responses.

dependencies.name: Workflow, Tasks and Alerts
dependencies.description: Tasks for rejections and document gating.
dependencies.how: Creates tasks and blocks documents until all lines are confirmed.

steps.title: Share passenger and room data with the DMC
keyFacts: Closer to departure the DMC receives the passenger list, room list and wishes for the confirmed services, generated from the same file data.
Only data needed for the service is shared, per supplier.
painPoints: Room lists sent to DMCs by spreadsheet diverge from the hotel lists sent by the operator.
Oversharing passenger data with every supplier is a privacy exposure.

dependencies.name: Passenger Data and Operational Lists
dependencies.description: Passenger and room data per supplier.
dependencies.how: Generates supplier-specific passenger lists.

dependencies.name: Supplier and DMC Portal
dependencies.how: Publishes the lists to the DMC.

steps.title: Propagate operator changes one to one to the DMC
keyFacts: A change on the file (extra passenger, changed room type, cancelled excursion) creates a versioned change request for the affected line only.
The DMC acknowledges the change in the portal; unacknowledged changes are escalated by workflow.
painPoints: Changes communicated in an email thread are the leading cause of DMC service errors.
Without acknowledgement, the operator assumes the DMC knows.

dependencies.name: Supplier Management and Communication
dependencies.how: Creates change deltas per affected line.

dependencies.name: Supplier and DMC Portal
dependencies.how: Lets the DMC acknowledge or dispute the change.

steps.title: The DMC reports delivery and invoices the operator
keyFacts: After the service the DMC marks delivery, reports no-shows and uploads its invoice against the confirmed lines.
Invoice lines matched to confirmed service lines make the operator's supplier settlement a check, not a reconstruction.
painPoints: Invoices that do not reference the request cannot be matched.
No-shows unreported by the DMC are invoiced anyway.

dependencies.name: Supplier and DMC Portal
dependencies.how: Captures delivery and the supplier invoice.

painPoints: Specialists tracking confirmations in a notebook lose lines.
Instant-confirm suppliers mixed with slow ones hide where the risk is.

Request texts are templated per supplier language.

Requests in the wrong language get slower answers.

The AI assistant drafts follow-up messages and flags supplier replies that need a decision.

Inbox triage of supplier replies eats the specialist's morning.

keyFacts: Replies from portal and API update lines automatically; email replies are attached to the line and confirmed with one click.
Alternatives are re-priced and, if the price changes, the client is informed via the portal.

Supplier references are printed on vouchers so the traveler can prove the booking on site.

Vouchers without supplier references are refused at reception.

Disputes without history are settled at the operator's cost.

rootGroups.name: Finance and Compliance Journeys
rootGroups.description: Collecting customer money, settling suppliers and flights, posting to accounting, reporting to the guarantee fund and closing the month from one system of record.

streams.name: Collect Payments and Invoice
streams.description: Take every booking from confirmation to fully paid: issue deposit and balance invoices from the file, send payment links, let travelers and resellers pay in the portal, match incoming payments automatically, remind before the due date and alert after it, and keep the receivables position current for finance without spreadsheets.
outcomes: Lower overdue receivables, because reminders and payment links run on schedule and payment status is visible per file
Invoice accuracy at first issue, since invoices are generated from the booking lines and change with them
Less finance handling time per booking, because payments are matched to invoices automatically

flows.title: From Deposit to Final Payment
flows.description: The standard collection cycle of a package booking: deposit at booking, balance six to eight weeks before departure, automatic reminders and matching.
flows.trigger: A booking is confirmed and the deposit invoice is due.
flows.successSignal: The booking is fully paid before the balance due date, with every payment matched to its invoice and visible in the file.

steps.title: Issue the deposit invoice from the booking
keyFacts: The deposit invoice is generated from the file with the deposit percentage from the conditions, the SGR contribution and any insurance premium as separate lines.
Invoice numbering, VAT treatment (including the travel agents' margin scheme where applicable) and layout are configured per tenant.
painPoints: Invoices typed in a separate accounting tool differ from the booking.
Wrong VAT treatment on travel invoices is a recurring audit finding.

dependencies.name: Booking Files and Dossiers

keyFacts: The invoice email carries a hosted payment link; iDEAL is the dominant method for Dutch consumers and settles within seconds.
Travelers can also pay from the my-trip portal, where the open amount is always current.
painPoints: Bank transfers with free-text references are matched by hand.
Portals that show a stale open amount cause double payments.

keyFacts: Payments via links are matched instantly; bank transfers are matched on invoice number, amount and payer with a review queue for exceptions.
Partial payments and overpayments are handled by rule and shown on the file.
painPoints: Manual matching of hundreds of transfers per week is the most tedious finance task at an operator.
Unmatched payments trigger reminders to customers who already paid.

Reminder tone and timing are configurable per tenant and customer type.
painPoints: Reminders sent by hand are late or forgotten in the high season.
One-size reminders annoy good customers and do not move late ones.

dependencies.name: Workflow, Tasks and Alerts

steps.title: Alert the desk on overdue balances

Departures with unpaid files are visible to operations, since unpaid travelers should not receive documents.
painPoints: Overdue lists exported weekly are outdated by the time someone calls.
Documents issued to unpaid travelers remove the last leverage.

streams.name: Settle Suppliers and Close Books
streams.description: Take the finance lead from supplier invoices, DMC statements and flight settlement files to matched purchase entries, correct margins per file, accounting entries in Exact, guarantee-fund reporting and a closed month — without rebuilding the trade's numbers in spreadsheets.
outcomes: Fewer days to close the monthly books, because purchase, sales and payment entries are posted from the ERP into accounting
Accurate supplier settlement, because supplier invoices are matched to confirmed service lines and flight tickets to settlement files
Guarantee-fund and package-travel obligations reported from system data rather than reconstructed

flows.successSignal: All supplier invoices are matched or disputed, flight tickets reconcile with the settlement file, and purchase entries are posted.

painPoints: Invoices in a shared mailbox are matched by memory and often twice.
Invoices without references need a call to the supplier.

Disputes without the original request take weeks.

rootGroups.name: Traveler, Market and Steering Journeys
rootGroups.description: Serving the traveler before, during and after the trip, marketing and retention under the operator's own brand, distribution through resellers and partners, and steering the business with BI and forecasts.

streams.name: Serve Travelers Before, During and After the Trip
streams.description: Take a traveler from booking confirmation to a completed, reviewed trip: complete passenger details and wishes in the my-trip portal, receive documents and itineraries at the right moment, travel with the app and in-trip updates, get help when something goes wrong, and share feedback through surveys and reviews that feed quality and marketing.
outcomes: Higher document self-service, because travelers download documents and complete data in the portal instead of calling
Higher traveler satisfaction, because information arrives on time on the device the traveler uses
Complaints and surveys closed in the system, feeding quality improvement and reviews rather than an inbox

flows.title: From Confirmation to Departure in the Traveler Portal
flows.description: The pre-trip service journey: portal access, data completion, ancillaries, documents and the pre-departure briefing.
flows.trigger: The traveler receives the booking confirmation with a portal link.
flows.successSignal: The traveler has completed all data, paid, downloaded the documents and installed the app before departure without contacting the desk.

steps.title: Activate the my-trip portal
keyFacts: The traveler activates access to the personal environment where booking, invoices, documents and tasks are visible.
The portal is branded per tenant so the traveler sees the operator's brand, not the software vendor's.
painPoints: Travelers emailing 'where is my booking' is the most common desk question.
Unbranded portals confuse travelers who booked with a brand.

dependencies.name: Traveler Portal and My-Trip App
dependencies.how: Provides the branded personal environment.

steps.title: Complete passenger details and wishes
keyFacts: Passport data, dietary wishes, mobility needs and emergency contacts are completed in the portal with deadlines set by workflow.
Validation catches names that differ from the passport, which matters for flight tickets.
painPoints: Passport data collected by email is a privacy and accuracy problem.
Name mismatches discovered at ticketing cost rebooking fees.

dependencies.name: Traveler Portal and My-Trip App
dependencies.description: Data completion tasks in the portal.
dependencies.how: Collects passenger data from the traveler.

dependencies.name: Passenger Data and Operational Lists
dependencies.how: Stores the completed data for lists and tickets.

steps.title: Add ancillaries such as excursions, insurance and eSIM
keyFacts: Ancillaries can be added after booking in the portal; an eSIM for the destination is offered via the Hubby partnership and delivered digitally.
Each addition creates an invoice line and, where needed, a supplier request.
painPoints: Ancillaries sold only at booking miss the traveler's later needs.
Additions handled by the desk are re-keyed and often missing from documents.

dependencies.name: Traveler Portal and My-Trip App
dependencies.how: Offers and sells post-booking extras.

dependencies.name: Booking Files and Dossiers
dependencies.how: Adds lines and triggers invoicing.

dependencies.name: Hubby eSIM
dependencies.description: Adds a destination eSIM to the trip as an ancillary and delivers activation details in the portal.
dependencies.interface: eSIM order and activation API
dependencies.how: Orders and activates the destination eSIM for the traveler.

steps.title: Receive travel documents on schedule
keyFacts: Documents are published in the portal and pushed to the app at a configured number of days before departure, once the file is paid and confirmed.
The traveler is notified by email and push and can download or view documents offline.
painPoints: Documents by post or as email attachments are lost and outdated.
Travelers unsure whether documents were sent call the desk.

dependencies.name: Travel Documents and Itinerary Delivery
dependencies.how: Generates and publishes documents on schedule.

dependencies.name: Traveler Portal and My-Trip App
dependencies.how: Makes documents available to the traveler.

steps.title: Install the app and view the itinerary
keyFacts: The itinerary, hotel details, pickup times and guide contact are available in a branded partner app fed from the ERP.
App content updates automatically when the file changes.
painPoints: Printed itineraries cannot change after printing.
Apps not connected to the back office show wrong information.

dependencies.name: Traveler Portal and My-Trip App
dependencies.how: Publishes itinerary data to the app.

dependencies.name: Integration Hub and Partner APIs
dependencies.how: Delivers the itinerary feed to partner apps.

dependencies.name: Travelia and Appit Traveler Apps

dependencies.interface: Itinerary and document feed API
dependencies.how: Renders the itinerary and documents in the branded traveler app.

steps.title: Receive the pre-departure briefing
keyFacts: A pre-departure message with weather, packing tips, meeting point and guide name is sent from a template per product.
Group travelers see their seat and pickup; tailor-made travelers see their first transfer details.
painPoints: Generic briefings ignore the specifics of the trip.
Missing meeting-point information is the top departure-day call.

dependencies.name: Email and Telephony Integration
dependencies.how: Sends the templated briefing.

dependencies.name: Travel Documents and Itinerary Delivery
dependencies.how: Supplies seat, pickup and transfer details.

steps.title: Ask a question and get an answer from the booking view
keyFacts: Questions asked in the portal or by email land on the file; the agent answers from one booking view with the full history.
AI assistance drafts answers to routine questions from the file data for the agent to approve.
painPoints: Questions answered without the file lead to contradictions.
Routine questions consume agent time that should go to sales.

dependencies.name: Traveler Portal and My-Trip App
dependencies.how: Captures traveler questions against the file.

dependencies.name: Email and Telephony Integration
dependencies.how: Links replies to the file.

flows.title: In-Trip Support and Aftercare
flows.description: The journey during and after travel: in-trip updates, incidents and complaints, surveys, reviews and retention hand-off.
flows.successSignal: The trip is completed with incidents resolved, the survey answered, a review published and the traveler flagged for the next campaign.

steps.title: Receive in-trip updates and changes
keyFacts: Changes during the trip — a changed pickup time, a hotel swap — are pushed to the app and portal from the file, and the guide sees the same information.
Emergency messages reach all participants of a departure at once.
painPoints: Updates by phone to each traveler do not scale during an incident.
Guides and travelers with different information create confusion.

dependencies.name: Traveler Portal and My-Trip App
dependencies.how: Delivers changes to travelers.

dependencies.name: Guide and Group Leader Portal
dependencies.description: Guide view of the same changes.
dependencies.how: Keeps the guide in sync with travelers.

dependencies.interface: Itinerary and document feed API
dependencies.how: Pushes in-trip notifications to the traveler app.

steps.title: Report an incident or complaint on tour
keyFacts: Incidents reported by the guide or the traveler are logged against the file with photos and time, and routed to the responsible agent.
Serious incidents trigger the emergency workflow with escalation to management.
painPoints: Complaints made verbally to the guide never reach the office.
Late incident logging weakens the operator's position with suppliers.

dependencies.name: Quality, Complaints, Surveys and Reviews
dependencies.how: Records incidents against the file.

dependencies.name: Guide and Group Leader Portal
dependencies.how: Lets the guide log incidents in the portal.

steps.title: Resolve the complaint and settle compensation
keyFacts: Complaints follow a defined process with response deadlines; compensation is recorded on the file and recovered from the supplier where applicable.
Outcomes feed supplier quality scores.
painPoints: Complaints handled in email threads miss response deadlines under trade codes.
Compensation paid but not recovered from suppliers erodes margin.

dependencies.name: Quality, Complaints, Surveys and Reviews
dependencies.how: Manages the complaint to resolution.

steps.title: Answer the post-trip survey
keyFacts: A survey is sent a few days after return; results are stored per departure, hotel, guide and component.
Low scores create a task for follow-up before a public review appears.
painPoints: Surveys in a separate tool cannot be linked to hotels or guides.
Unhappy travelers not contacted write the public review first.

dependencies.name: Quality, Complaints, Surveys and Reviews
dependencies.how: Sends surveys and stores results.

dependencies.name: Workflow, Tasks and Alerts
dependencies.how: Creates tasks for low ratings.

steps.title: Invite a public review
keyFacts: Satisfied travelers are invited to review on Trustpilot; reviews are shown on the website next to the product.
Invitation timing is tuned to the survey response.
painPoints: Review invitations sent to everyone amplify the unhappy minority.
Reviews not shown on product pages are wasted conversion power.

dependencies.name: Quality, Complaints, Surveys and Reviews
dependencies.how: Triggers review invitations after positive surveys.

steps.title: Hand the traveler off to retention

Consent captured at booking governs which campaigns the traveler receives.
painPoints: Returning travelers treated as new leads waste the relationship.
Campaigns without consent tracking breach GDPR.

streams.name: Market and Retain Customers
streams.description: Take the owner and marketing lead from CRM data to campaigns and repeat bookings: build segments from booking history, interests and consent, run email campaigns through Spotler, publish reviews and inspiration on the website, measure conversion back to bookings, and turn past travelers into repeat bookers under the operator's own brand.
outcomes: Higher direct online sales under the own brand, because campaigns land on a real-time bookable website
Higher repeat booking rate, because segments are built from actual travel history and trip completion
Campaign results measured in bookings and margin, not opens and clicks

flows.title: Segment, Campaign and Convert
flows.description: From a marketing goal to a measured campaign: define the segment, sync to Spotler, send, land on the website and attribute bookings.
flows.trigger: The owner wants to fill the spring departures of a coach series that is at 40% load.
flows.successSignal: The campaign is sent to the right segment, bookings are attributed to it and the load factor of the target departures rises.

steps.title: Define the campaign goal and segment
keyFacts: Segments combine booking history (destination, product type, travel month), value, survey score and consent status from the CRM.
The segment size and expected response are shown before sending.
painPoints: Mass mailings to the whole database hurt deliverability and brand.
Segments built in the mail tool lack booking data.

dependencies.name: Email Marketing and Segmentation
dependencies.how: Defines segments with consent applied.

dependencies.name: CRM and Contact Management
dependencies.how: Provides the attributes for segmentation.

steps.title: Select the products and offers to promote
keyFacts: Underperforming departures and their current price tier are selected from the load-factor view; offers are configured as time-limited price tiers.
Offers are visible on the website and at the desk at the same time.
painPoints: Offers announced by email but not applied at the desk anger customers.
Promoting departures that are already full wastes attention.

dependencies.name: Departures and Capacity Management
dependencies.how: Identifies departures to promote.

dependencies.name: Pricing, Yield and Group Calculations
dependencies.how: Creates time-limited offers.

steps.title: Draft the campaign content with the AI assistant
keyFacts: The assistant drafts subject lines and copy from the product content and the segment profile in the tenant's tone.
Drafts are reviewed and edited; nothing is sent automatically.
painPoints: Copywriting bottlenecks delay campaigns past the booking window.
Generic copy ignores what the segment has already travelled.

dependencies.name: AI Office Assistants
dependencies.how: Generates draft copy from product and segment data.

steps.title: Sync the segment and send through Spotler
keyFacts: The segment is synced to Spotler with consent flags; the campaign is sent and engagement flows back to the contact records.
Unsubscribes are written back to the CRM immediately.
painPoints: Lists exported to the mail tool drift from the CRM.
Unsubscribes not synced back lead to GDPR complaints.

dependencies.name: Email Marketing and Segmentation
dependencies.how: Syncs segments and returns engagement.

dependencies.name: Spotler Email Marketing
dependencies.description: Runs email campaigns on segments exported from the CRM and returns engagement data.
dependencies.interface: Contact and segment sync, campaign statistics
dependencies.how: Sends the campaign and returns opens, clicks and unsubscribes.

steps.title: Land on real-time bookable landing pages
keyFacts: Campaign links land on product pages with live availability, the offer price and reviews, and the traveler can book without a call.
Campaign parameters are stored on the booking for attribution.
painPoints: Landing pages with 'request a quote' lose most of the campaign's momentum.
Bookings without campaign attribution make marketing spend unmeasurable.

dependencies.name: Customer Website, CMS and Online Booking
dependencies.how: Renders bookable offers with attribution.

dependencies.name: Booking Files and Dossiers
dependencies.how: Stores the campaign source on the file.

steps.title: Measure bookings and margin per campaign
keyFacts: Dashboards show bookings, revenue and margin per campaign and segment, and the load-factor change of the promoted departures.
Results feed the next segment definition.
painPoints: Open and click rates say nothing about margin.
Campaign effects unknown per departure repeat the same discount mistakes.

dependencies.name: Business Intelligence and Reporting
dependencies.how: Attributes bookings and margin to campaigns.

dependencies.name: Email Marketing and Segmentation
dependencies.how: Links engagement to booking outcomes.

streams.name: Distribute Through Resellers and Partners
streams.description: Take the operator's products to reseller agents, independent agents and partner channels: give resellers a portal to book, quote and retrieve documents for their clients without phone calls, feed products to partner channels through the integration hub, import partner bookings into the same booking files, and settle commissions correctly.
outcomes: Higher portal booking share among resellers, because the portal shows the same live availability, seats and prices as the desk
Lower reseller handling time per booking, since quotes, documents and changes are self-service
Partner channel bookings that arrive as normal booking files, not emails to re-key

flows.title: A Reseller Books a Product in the Portal
flows.description: A travel agent books an operator's group tour for a client in the reseller portal, from availability check to documents.
flows.trigger: A client of a retail travel agent asks for a specific coach tour date.
flows.successSignal: The reseller has booked, the client's documents are retrievable in the portal and the commission is recorded, without a call to the operator.

steps.title: Log in with the agency account
keyFacts: Reseller users belong to an agency with agreed commission and payment terms; access rights are managed per agency by the operator.
Independent (ZRA-style) agents are supported as one-person agencies.
painPoints: Shared logins make it impossible to know who booked.
Onboarding agencies by hand delays new distribution.

dependencies.name: Identity, Tenants and Access
dependencies.how: Authenticates reseller users per agency.

dependencies.name: Reseller and Agent Portal
dependencies.how: Holds commission and payment terms.

steps.title: Search availability and see net or gross prices
keyFacts: The portal shows live availability, seat map and either gross price with commission or net price, according to the agency terms.
Product content and photos come from the same catalogue as the website.
painPoints: Resellers calling to check availability defeat the purpose of a portal.
Portals with brochure prices only cannot close a sale.

dependencies.name: Pricing, Yield and Group Calculations
dependencies.how: Applies agency pricing rules.

dependencies.name: Components, Inventory and Availability
dependencies.how: Supplies seats and rooms available.

steps.title: Quote the client from the portal
keyFacts: A branded quote for the client, with the agency's own logo, is generated from the portal and can be turned into a booking later.
Options hold capacity for the reseller for a limited time.
painPoints: Quotes typed by the agent contain wrong inclusions.
Without options, the seat is gone when the client decides.

dependencies.name: Reseller and Agent Portal
dependencies.how: Creates quotes and options for the agency.

dependencies.name: Booking Files and Dossiers
dependencies.how: Holds capacity as an option.

steps.title: Book and enter the client's passengers
keyFacts: The reseller books with passenger data, seat and wishes; the booking file is created with the agency as booker and the passengers as travelers.
The operator's desk sees the booking like any other file.
painPoints: Bookings emailed by resellers are re-keyed by the desk.
Files that mix agency and traveler contact data confuse communication.

Payment terms may allow the agency to pay at balance date only.
painPoints: Invoices sent to the traveler instead of the agency breach the agency relationship.
Commission errors are the main cause of reseller disputes.

dependencies.name: Invoicing, Payment Links and Collection

dependencies.name: Reseller and Agent Portal
dependencies.how: Provides the invoicing model.

Changes made by the operator are visible in the portal with notifications.
painPoints: Resellers asking the operator for documents by phone cost both sides time.
Clients receiving documents with a brand they never dealt with are confused.

The operator's operations lists update automatically.

streams.name: Steer the Travel Business with Insight
streams.description: Take the owner and finance lead from transaction data — bookings, departures, invoices, supplier costs, campaigns — to BI dashboards, margin analysis, demand forecasts and KPI steering, so that capacity, pricing and headcount decisions are made on the platform's numbers rather than on gut feel and spreadsheets.
outcomes: Revenue per FTE tracked and improved, because the owner sees where handling time goes and which processes scale
Capacity and pricing decisions taken on load-factor and margin data per departure, weeks earlier than before
One set of numbers shared by sales, operations and finance, closing the gap between sold and realised margin

flows.title: From Transaction Data to Weekly Steering
flows.description: The recurring steering loop: data refresh, dashboards, KPI review, decisions and actions back into the operation.
flows.trigger: The weekly management meeting is scheduled and the dashboards refresh overnight.
flows.successSignal: Decisions on pricing, capacity and follow-up are taken from the dashboards and turned into tasks and rule changes in the ERP.

steps.title: Refresh the analytical data model
keyFacts: Bookings, departures, invoices, payments, supplier costs, campaigns and complaints are loaded nightly into the analytical model, per tenant.
Definitions (booking, passenger, revenue, margin) are fixed once so every dashboard uses the same numbers.
painPoints: Exports to Excel every Monday produce a different number per person.
Undefined metrics turn every meeting into a debate about the data.

dependencies.name: Business Intelligence and Reporting
dependencies.how: Loads and harmonises the data nightly.

dependencies.name: Invoicing, Payment Links and Collection
dependencies.how: Supplies revenue and receivables.

steps.title: Review the north-star KPIs
keyFacts: The owner dashboard shows revenue per FTE, operating margin, online booking share, quote-to-booking conversion and days to close, with trends and targets.
Each KPI drills down to the departures, agents or products behind it.
painPoints: KPIs presented once a quarter are too late to act on the season.
Dashboards without drill-down invite speculation about causes.

dependencies.name: Business Intelligence and Reporting

dependencies.how: Provides trade-specific dashboards embedded in the ERP.

steps.title: Analyse margin and load factor per departure and product
keyFacts: Sold versus realised margin and load factor per departure identify products to reprice, merge or drop.
Supplier cost trends highlight contracts to renegotiate.
painPoints: Product decisions made on revenue alone keep loss-making departures alive.
Supplier cost creep unnoticed erodes a whole season.

dependencies.name: Business Intelligence and Reporting
dependencies.how: Analyses margin and load per departure.

dependencies.name: Accounting Integration and Supplier Settlement
dependencies.how: Supplies matched purchase costs.

steps.title: Analyse sales and service performance per agent and channel
keyFacts: Conversion, handling time, first-contact resolution and proposal turnaround are shown per agent, specialist and channel.
Complaint and survey scores per guide, hotel and product complete the picture.
painPoints: Agents judged on booking counts alone ignore margin and service.
Service quality unmeasured per supplier repeats bad choices.

dependencies.name: Business Intelligence and Reporting
dependencies.how: Reports per agent, channel and supplier.

dependencies.name: CRM and Contact Management
dependencies.how: Supplies conversion and handling data.

steps.title: Decide and turn decisions into actions
keyFacts: Decisions become concrete changes: a price tier adjusted, a departure merged, a supplier flagged, a follow-up campaign — each created as a rule change or a task from the meeting.
The AI assistant summarises the week's anomalies and proposes actions for review.
painPoints: Decisions minuted but not executed are the norm without a task system.
Owners drowning in dashboards need a summary, not more charts.

dependencies.name: Pricing, Yield and Group Calculations

Thresholds alert the owner before a risk becomes a regulatory or cash problem.
painPoints: Risk seen only in the annual audit is seen too late.
Exposure to the guarantee fund unknown surprises the owner at contribution time.
